title: Relational Graph Transformer
one_liner: A transformer-based architecture that tokenizes relational database tables as heterogeneous temporal graphs, capturing long-range patterns that message-passing networks cannot see.
lead: Databases organize data in multiple related tables (customers, purchases, products). Graph neural networks struggle with this setup: they treat it like a network of connections, but miss patterns that skip over intermediate nodes. This paper introduces a transformer (a model that attends freely to every input at once) designed specifically for database tables, using a five-part representation to convert each database row into a labeled package that preserves what table it comes from, when it was created, and how it connects to its neighbors.

paras: When you turn a database into a graph — customers as nodes, purchases as edges connecting them to products — a standard graph neural network works by having each node swap messages with its immediate neighbors, then neighbors-of-neighbors. The problem: some patterns live far apart. A product purchased by customer A, who is similar to customer B, reveals something about what B should buy — but customer B never directly talks to that product. The message would have to bounce through intermediaries (product through first customer through second customer through more customers). By then, it gets scrambled by each hop.

The naive approach is to make the network deeper to reach farther. This fails because deep message-passing networks get tangled with their own signals (each new layer blurs what came from where), and they still cannot freely see across the table the way a database query does. You are stuck: capture local patterns in 2-3 hops, or risk noise.

callout.html: Instead of messages bouncing through the graph, turn the database into a list of tokens (one token per row, broken into five parts: the row's data, which table it came from, how far it is from the query row, when it was created, and a quick look at its neighbors), then use a transformer—a model that attends freely to every token at once.

steps.text: For each row, grab its closest K neighbors within 2 hops, respecting timestamps to avoid cheating.
Turn each neighbor row into five tokens: encoded data values, which table it belongs to, hop distance, time delta, a random graph structure sample.
Let the query row focus on its own neighbors; this builds a fine-grained local picture.
Pool all query rows across the database into summary centroids; every row can also focus on these global summaries.
Use the combined local and global representations to make the prediction.

paras: The paper changes how each node in a relational graph is represented. Instead of a single vector of learned features, each node becomes a five-element tuple: its row data, its table identity, its distance in hops, its timestamp, and a random sample of its local graph structure. This tuple is then encoded into five separate numerical representations and combined into a single token.

hidden.name: structural accessibility
paras: Structural accessibility is how easy it is for a far-away pattern to influence a prediction. In a message-passing network, a product five hops away from your query row can only send a signal if it survives five noisy bounces. In a transformer, every token is immediately accessible. The paper does not measure this as a single number (like signal-to-noise ratio), but it is the reason the method works: it measures and uses access directly.

RelGT estimates accessibility by the distance (hop count) and timestamp information baked into each token, then lets the transformer learn which distances and times matter. A weight in the transformer can learn to ignore products from two years ago (stale signal) and focus on fresh purchases from 1-2 hops away (relevant neighbors).

heat.caption: Darker means easier to reach and combine. Message-passing fades over hops; tokenization preserves everything.

reads.html: In a database, a product you bought last month is directly relevant to what you will buy next month. A message-passing graph has to bounce that signal through other customers, losing it along the way. The paper preserves the signal by making every token visible, labeled with its timestamp and distance—so the transformer model can see and use it.

Hop distance, time difference, and node type are each converted into a list of numbers and stacked together into one big bundle. This allows the transformer to learn which combinations predict relevance. Message-passing gets noisier the farther you go, because each hop mixes the signal with the current state at each node; stacking bundles avoids this because every piece of information is separate and labeled.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: Direct access + context tags
paras: The transformer can attend to any token, but it needs to know which tokens matter. The five-part tokenization gives every token a context tag: its table (product vs. customer), distance from the query (1 hop vs. 3 hops), and age (yesterday vs. 1 year ago). The transformer then learns: 'attention to product tokens 1-2 hops old predicts well; skip tokens older than 1 year.'

In contrast, a message-passing network has to compress all that information into a single updated vector as the message bounces through neighbors. By the time a product five hops away sends its signal, the signal has been mixed with the intermediate customers' current state, noise creeps in, and the transformer at the top sees a blurry average. RelGT avoids this: every product and customer is a separate token, each labeled with its own metadata, and the transformer picks out the clean ones.

stages.s: Relational table rows sampled within 2 hops.
Multi-element tokenization: five encoders (data, type, hop distance, time, structure).
Local attention: query row attends to its K neighbors.
Global attention: all rows attend to pooled database summaries.

math.words: token equals concatenate of five encodings of node data, node type, hop distance, time difference, and a random sampled subgraph structure
math.equation: t_j = concat(encode_feat(x_j), encode_type(phi_j), encode_hop(p_j), encode_time(tau_j - tau_i), encode_structure(Z_j))
symbols: the row's data (numerical and categorical features)
which table this node comes from (node type)
hop distance from query node i to neighbor j
time difference between node j and query node i
a random sample of j's local graph structure
stack the five encodings end-to-end into one long vector

worked.title: A concrete example
lines: Suppose we are predicting for customer Alice (node i, time=2025-01-01).
Neighbor product X (node j) has: data=[price=100, rating=4.2], type=product, hops=1, time=2024-12-15.
encode_feat([100,4.2]) = [0.8, 0.6] (a 2-dim list of numbers; real model uses d=64).
encode_type(product) = [0.1, 0.2, 0.0, ...] (a learned representation of 'product', distinct from 'customer').
The transformer can now see: 'this is a product, close by, recent, with these properties' and decide to attend to it.

math.note: The five encodings preserve different dimensions of a database row: what it contains, which table, how far, how old, and its graph shape. The transformer learns which combinations predict well.

charts.title: Message-passing baseline (GraphSAGE)
charts.note: Standard GNN bounces messages 2-3 hops; misses long-range patterns.

charts.title: Relational Graph Transformer
charts.note: Direct token access + metadata tags let the model see and use distant patterns. Improvements up to 18% on RelBench tasks.

items.html: If you accidentally include future rows (timestamps after the query date), the model learns to cheat. The paper guards this by filtering neighbors to only include those created before or at the same time as the query row, but a buggy implementation can break this safeguard.
The method samples a fixed K neighbors. If a row has fewer than K neighbors, it fills with random nodes. If many rows are isolated (no neighbors in 2 hops), the model wastes tokens on noise.

Local attention over K tokens is cheap, but global attention pools over ALL rows. On a database with billions of rows, creating a centroid for every subset becomes slow. The paper tests on medium-scale RelBench; real financial databases may hit limits.

Enforce strict temporal ordering when constructing neighborhoods. Tune K (neighborhood size) and global centroid count to your data size. Validate that improvements persist on out-of-distribution future data (time shift test).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small two-table database: customers (with age, location, past purchases) and products (with price, category, rating). Create a prediction task: given a customer, predict their next purchase category. Train a message-passing GNN baseline (e.g., PyTorch Geometric's GraphSAGE on a relational graph) and a Relational Graph Transformer side by side. Measure accuracy on the held-out test set. Also measure how well each model predicts for customers whose favorite product is 3+ hops away in the graph (i.e., only reachable through multiple intermediate nodes). The transformer should win the far-field test; the GNN should lose accuracy when the pattern lives far away.
demo.closing: The transformer's token and metadata design makes it immune to long-distance decay because every token stays clear and labeled, rather than getting mixed with intermediate states as messages bounce through the graph. This demo makes that visible: one model sees the far-away patterns, the other does not.
